# R and RStudio

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/code_window.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Programming is a Superpower

-   Programming is how we talk to and control computers

-   It gives us power and flexibility

-   Everything in this course is done via programming

-   Programming will leave a record of what we did (i.e., code), so we can later reuse, adapt, and share it


## R and Other Stats Software {.fs80}

-   You may have met [SPSS]{.b .blue}, [SAS]{.b .blue}, [Stata]{.b .blue}, [Mplus]{.b .blue}, [JASP]{.b .blue}, or [jamovi]{.b .blue}
    -   All of them can run the analyses in this course

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   R is [free]{.b .green}, on every computer you will ever use
    -   No licence to buy, renew, or lose when you change institution
    -   JASP and jamovi are free too, and both are built on R
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   R is a [real programming language]{.b .green}, not a menu with a syntax window
    -   Which is why [data preparation]{.b .blue} (cleaning, reshaping,
        merging) is easier
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   New methods arrive as [packages]{.b .blue}, years before commercial tools do
:::


## The R Ecosystem {.fs80}

1.  Your [computer]{.b .blue} is the [engine]{.b .green} of a car
    -   It provides raw power for computation

::: {.fragment .mt1}
2.  The [R language]{.b .blue} is the [controls]{.b .green}
    -   It lets you apply and direct that power
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
3.  [RStudio]{.b .blue} is like a fancy [dashboard]{.b .green} for the car
    -   It adds information and convenience
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
4.  An [R package]{.b .blue} is like an [add-on]{.b .green} for the car
    -   It adds new features and capabilities
:::


## Installing R {.fs80}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column .pr4 width="50%"}
#### Windows

1.  Open a web browser
2.  Visit [cloud.r-project.org](https://cloud.r-project.org)
3.  Click "Download R for Windows"
4.  Click the "base" subdirectory link
5.  Click "Download R-4.X.X" (e.g., 4.6.1)
6.  Run the downloaded .exe file
7.  Select all the default options
8.  Complete the installation wizard
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Mac OS

1.  Open a web browser
2.  Visit [cloud.r-project.org](https://cloud.r-project.org)
3.  Click "Download R for macOS"
4.  Click "R-4.X.X-arm64.pkg" (Apple silicon) or "R-4.X.X-x86_64.pkg" (older Intel Macs)
5.  Run the downloaded .pkg file
6.  Select all the default options
7.  Complete the installation wizard
:::
:::

::: aside
*Note.* You will need to repeat this process every time a new version of R is released (every 4–5 months).
:::


## Installing RStudio {.fs80}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column .pr4 width="50%"}
#### Windows

1.  Open a web browser
2.  Visit [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/){preview-link="false"}
3.  Scroll down to the **RStudio IDE** table
4.  Find the row for "Windows"
5.  Click "RStudio-2026.XX.X-XXX.exe"
6.  Run the downloaded .exe file
7.  Select all the default options
8.  Complete the installation wizard
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Mac OS

1.  Open a web browser
2.  Visit [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/){preview-link="false"}
3.  Scroll down to the **RStudio IDE** table
4.  Find the row for "macOS 13+"
5.  Click "RStudio-2026.XX.X-XXX.dmg"
6.  Run the downloaded .dmg file
7.  Drag the RStudio icon to your Applications folder (if you want)
:::
:::

::: aside
*Note.* You will need to repeat this process every time a new version of RStudio is released (every 2–4 months).
:::


## RStudio Window

![](../../img/rstudio_labels.jpg)


::: aside
*Note.* You can customize RStudio (e.g., the fonts, color themes, and pane layout) under "Tools \> Global Options".
:::


# Console

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/terminal.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## R will Grant your Wishes {.fs80}

-   R is a [well-meaning]{.b .green} but [overly literal]{.b .green} genie

    -   It has the power to grant almost any wish
    -   But we must phrase our wishes carefully!
    -   *We will always get what we ask for...*
    -   *...but not always what we wanted.*

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Mastering the [R language]{.b .blue} means learning...

    -   How to properly phrase commands
    -   How to decipher error messages
    -   How to view code from R's perspective
    -   How to find and fix small mistakes
:::


## Communicating with R {.fs70}

-   The [Console]{.b .blue} is like a [chat window]{.b .green} with R
    -   You send a command to R and get a response
    -   Neither side of the conversation is saved

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   An [R Script]{.b .blue} is like an [email thread]{.b .green} with R
    -   You send many commands to R all at once
    -   Only your side of the conversation is saved
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   A [Quarto Document]{.b .blue} is like a [scrapbook]{.b .green} with R
    -   You can combine code and formatted text
    -   Both sides of the conversation are saved
:::


## Arithmetic


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
10 + 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
10 - 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 7
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
10 * 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 30
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
10 / 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.333333
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
10 ^ 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 100
```


:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
The four operators you already know, plus `^` for powers. Spaces are optional.
:::

## Pitfall: Notation R Does Not Accept


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
10 x 3
```
:::


::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected symbol in "10 x"
```
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
10 \ 3
```
:::


::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected '\' in "10 \"
```
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Multiplication is `*`, never `x`, and division is `/`, the slash that leans
the other way. R reads `\` as the start of something else entirely.
:::

## Order of Operations


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
10 + 3 * 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(10 + 3) * 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 26
```


:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
Multiplication happens before addition, exactly as in algebra. Parentheses
override that, and are worth adding whenever the order is not obvious.
:::

## Decimals and Negative Numbers


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
10 + -30
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -20
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
1.234
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.234
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
1 / 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.3333333
```


:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
Negative numbers need no special treatment, and division gives a decimal, not a
fraction. R prints as many digits as it thinks you need, not all it has.
:::

## How R Prints Numbers


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
09.870
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9.87
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
9876543
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9876543
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-line-numbers="false"}
9,876,543
```
:::


::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected ',' in "9,"
```
:::

::: {.takeaway}
R drops leading and trailing zeros that carry no information. Thousands
separators are for humans: type the digits and **nothing else**.
:::

# Scripts

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/edit_doc.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Creating a New Script

-   A script is just a [plain text file]{.b .blue} saved with a [`.R`]{.b .blue} extension
    -   Which makes it easy to [share your code]{.b .green} with other people
-   Any one of these will create one:
    -   [File > New File > R Script]{.b .blue}
    -   Top bar: the [white square with a green plus]{.b .blue} icon
    -   <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>N</kbd> (Win) or <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>N</kbd> (Mac)

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   A new pane appears, called the [Source Editor]{.b .green}
:::

## Entering Commands into a Script


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
(1.4 + 2.8 + 9.3) / 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
30.1 - 24.7
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 5.4
```


:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
A script holds many lines at once. Think of it as drafting an email with several
instructions rather than shouting one at a time.
:::

## Running One Line of Code

-   Hitting <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Return</kbd> [does not run the code]{.b .blue}; it just adds a new line

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   To run the line your cursor is on:
    -   Click the [Run]{.b .blue} button (top-right of the Source Editor)
    -   Or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> (Win) / <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Return</kbd> (Mac)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   The results appear down in the [Console]{.b .green}
:::

## Running Many Lines of Code

-   To run [several lines]{.b .blue} at once:
    -   Highlight them with the mouse, then click [Run]{.b .blue}
    -   Or highlight them and press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Return</kbd>

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   To run [the whole script]{.b .blue} at once:
    -   Click the [Source]{.b .blue} button (top-right)
    -   Or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Return</kbd>
:::

## Adding Comments to Scripts


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Calculate the average score on the quiz
(1.4 + 2.8 + 9.3) / 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
100 / 9 # a comment can also end a line
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 11.11111
```


:::
:::


::: {.takeaway}
Anything after a `#` is ignored by R and exists only for human readers. A comment
can sit on its own line or at the end of one; the code still runs.
:::

## Saving the Script File

-   Any one of these will do it:
    -   [File > Save]{.b .blue}
    -   Source bar: the [blue and white disk]{.b .blue} icon
    -   <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> (Win) or <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> (Mac)

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   For now, save it wherever; we will learn about [Projects]{.b .green} soon
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   You now have a [.R file]{.b .blue} you can keep or transfer
    -   Only the [code]{.b .green} is saved, not the results
:::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
